segments.heading: Header comment: the two modes
segments.text: The comment gives the two modes. `probe` builds the binaries, prints the machine code of the kernels and runs the self-test. `all` does the same and then runs the timed processes. The timed run of 2026-11-13 used `all` [Ref1].

- `-e`: the script stops at the first command that fails (exit status not 0). A failing command inside an `if` test or in front of `||` does not stop it.
- `-u`: the script stops when it uses a variable that was never set.
- `-o pipefail`: a pipeline (commands joined with `|`) counts as failed when any command of it fails, not only the last one.

segments.heading: Restart on CPUs 0 to 119
segments.text:
- The script starts itself again under `taskset -c 0-119`. This tool limits a command to CPUs 0 to 119.
- `exec` replaces the running shell with that command. No extra process is created.
- `_PINNED=1` is set for the new start. The test `-z ${_PINNED:-}` (is the variable empty or not set?) is then false. So the restart happens only once.
- Every process that the script starts later inherits the CPU limit. The compiler, the self-test and the benchmark binaries are among them.

- Line 10: `MODE` is the first argument. Without an argument it is `probe`.
- Line 11: `MARKER` is the path of the marker file.
- Line 12: the `case` accepts `probe` and `all`. Any other word prints the usage text and ends the script with status 2.

segments.heading: Function `check_marker`: stop when another test runs
segments.text: `check_marker` tests whether the marker file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` exists (`-e`). If it exists, the function prints a message to the error output (stderr, `>&2`) and ends the script with status 3. Line 14 is the first call.

- Line 15: `SRC` is the absolute path of the folder that holds this script. `dirname "$0"` gives the folder part of the script path. `cd` and `pwd` turn it into an absolute path.
- The sources are read from `SRC` and the binaries are written to `SRC`.
- Lines 16 to 18: `OUT` is a new result folder, `kernels-` plus the UTC time, under `$HOME/cache-perf/results`.

segments.heading: Compiler flags, one by one
segments.text:
- `-O3`: optimization level 3, the highest numbered level of gcc. At this level gcc may turn a scalar loop into a vector loop.
- `-march=native`: the target architecture is that of the machine that compiles, here CRB. The architecture decides which instructions gcc may use [Ref12]. A record from CRB of 2026-11-11 shows what the same gcc version picked for `native`: the architecture name `armv8-a` with 16 extensions (sets of extra instructions), among them four SVE2 extensions [Ref13]. The listing shows one case: two kernels of `bw_old` use SVE instructions [Ref1]. Line 19 has no `-mtune` and no `-mcpu` flag. For this case the gcc manual says that the code is tuned for a range of processors that implement the architecture [Ref12].
- `-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns`: turns off one step that `-O3` would run. That step replaces a loop pattern with a call to a library function, for example a copy loop with `memcpy`. With the flag, gcc does not replace a kernel loop with such a call.
- `-pthread`: compile and link with support for POSIX threads (the standard thread interface of Unix systems). The benchmark creates its threads with `pthread_create`.
- `-Wall`: turn on most warning messages. `-Wextra`: turn on some extra warnings. A warning does not change the machine code.
- `-std=gnu11`: the language is C of the 2011 standard with the GNU extensions.

segments.heading: Function `load`: the three load averages
segments.text: Function `load` prints the first three fields of `/proc/loadavg` (`cut -d' ' -f1-3`: split the line at spaces and keep fields 1 to 3). They are the load averages over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.

segments.heading: Start `probe.txt` with the build environment
segments.text:
- The braces group lines 22 to 26. `> "$OUT/probe.txt"` writes the output of all of them to the new file `probe.txt`.
- Line 22: host name, UTC time, load averages, number of login sessions (`who` prints one line per login session, `wc -l` counts the lines) and the mode.
- Line 23: the first line of `gcc --version`. It names the compiler version.
- Line 24: the flags of line 19.
- Line 25: the setting for transparent huge pages. The value in square brackets is the active one.
- Line 26: `ps -eo pcpu,user,comm --sort=-pcpu` lists all processes with their %CPU, user and command name, highest %CPU first. `head -6` keeps the title line and 5 processes.

segments.heading: Function `build`: one gcc call
segments.text:
- `build` runs `gcc` with the flags of line 19, followed by the arguments of the call (`"$@"`). `$CFLAGS` has no quotes. So the shell splits it into the seven flags.
- `2>>` appends the messages of gcc (its error output) to `build.txt`.
- If gcc fails, the script prints `build.txt` to the error output and ends with status 5.
- Line 30 creates `build.txt` as an empty file before the first build. `:` is a command that does nothing, and `>` empties the file.

segments.heading: Build the two benchmark binaries, the self-test and `probe.o`
segments.text:
- Line 31: `bandwidth.orig.c` (the old source) becomes the binary `bw_old`. It holds the old read kernel.
- Line 32: `bandwidth.c` (the new source) becomes the binary `bw_new`. It holds the new read kernel.
- Line 33: `selftest.c` becomes the binary `selftest`. This source includes `bandwidth.c`. So the self-test checks the kernels of the new source [Ref6].
- Line 34: `probe.c` becomes the object file `probe.o`. `-c` means compile only, with no linking. The file holds three candidate copy loops [Ref7].
- All four builds use the same flags. `-o` names the output file. All four output files are written to the script folder.
- Both modes run these lines. So every start of the script builds `bw_old` and `bw_new` again and replaces the files.
Append the size of `build.txt` in bytes to `probe.txt` (`wc -c` counts bytes). 0 bytes means that gcc printed no warning. On 2026-11-13 the size was 0 bytes [Ref1].

segments.heading: Append checksums and machine code to `probe.txt`
segments.text:
- The braces that open on line 36 close on line 53. `>> "$OUT/probe.txt"` there appends the output of lines 37 to 52 to `probe.txt`.
- Line 37: the sha256 of the four sources, of this script and of the three binaries. The parentheses run `cd` and `sha256sum` in a subshell (a child copy of the shell) inside `SRC`. So the output shows the file names without a folder.
- Line 38: the sha256 of the copy of the benchmark source in the folder `bench`. On 2026-11-13 it was equal to the sha256 of `bandwidth.orig.c` [Ref1].
- ra.sh later compares `bw_old` and `bw_new` with the two values that line 37 wrote [Ref8].

- For `bw_new`, then `bw_old`, and for each of the six kernel functions: print a title line `=== binary function ===`, then the machine code of that function.
- `objdump -d --disassemble=$f` prints the instructions of the function `$f` only. `--no-show-raw-insn` leaves out the bytes of each instruction.
- `sed -n '/>:$/,/^$/p'` prints only the lines from the function label (a line that ends with `>:`) to the next empty line. The title lines of objdump are dropped.
- This listing is the record of what each kernel does in one loop pass. The C source alone does not decide that. The compiler chooses the instructions.
The same listing for the three functions of `probe.o`. These loops are only compiled. No part of the script runs them.

- The same listing for the function `chase` of two other programs in the folder `bench`: `latency` and `homelat`.
- `objdump` fails when the binary is missing. `pipefail` then makes the pipeline fail. The part after `||` prints the line `(not available)`, and the script continues.
- The script only prints the machine code of these two programs. It does not run them.
- Line 53 closes the braces of line 36.

segments.heading: Run the self-test
segments.text:
- Line 54: check the marker file again.
- Line 55: run `selftest`. `> ... 2>&1` writes its output and its error output to `selftest.txt`.
- On success (`&&`) the script appends `## selftest exit=0` to `probe.txt`.
- On failure (`||`) it appends the exit status to `probe.txt`, prints `selftest failed` and the result folder, and ends with status 4.
- So the timed processes below start only after the self-test has passed.

In mode `probe` the script ends here with status 0. Before that it appends the load averages and the UTC time to `probe.txt` and prints the result folder. Only mode `all` continues to the timed processes.

segments.heading: Function `one`: start one benchmark process
segments.text:
- Arguments in this order: csv file, binary, kernel, threads, CPU list, bytes, round.
- Line 61: check the marker file before every process. Nothing checks it while a process runs.
- Line 62: append one line that starts with `-- ` to the csv file. It holds the arguments, the 1-minute load average at this moment and the UTC time. stat_k120.py reads this line to know which rows belong to which process [Ref10].
- Line 63: start the binary with one kernel (`--kernel`) and wait until it ends. `>>` appends the rows that the binary prints to the csv file.
- `--reps 3`: the process times 3 intervals. `--min-ms 500`: each interval lasts at least 500 ms [Ref3].
- If the binary ends with a status other than 0, `set -e` ends the script with that status.

`K1` is the kernel order of round 1. `K2` holds the same six names in the reverse order, for round 2. `read` and `asmread` are the read kernels, and the other four names are the write and copy kernels. A `for` loop over such a list takes the names one by one.

segments.heading: One-thread processes (the rerun of 2026-11-17 does not repeat them)
segments.text:
- Two rounds. In each round: CPU 0, then CPU 2. For each CPU the buffer sizes `32K`, `1M`, `8M` and `1G` (32 KiB, 1 MiB, 8 MiB, 1 GiB). For each size all six kernels with both binaries.
- Each process has 1 thread, pinned to that one CPU. Its rows are appended to `one-thread.csv`.
- That gives 2 x 2 x 4 x 6 x 2 = 192 processes.
- Round 2 reverses the order of the kernels and of the binaries, as in the 120-thread part. It does not reverse the order of the CPUs and of the sizes.
- Line 74 appends the load averages and the UTC time after this part to `probe.txt`.

segments.heading: The 120-thread part: the test that ra.sh repeats
segments.text:
- Round 1: for each kernel first `bw_old`, then `bw_new`. Order: old `read`, new `read`, old `write`, new `write`, old `copy`, new `copy`, old `asmread`, new `asmread`, old `asmwrite`, new `asmwrite`, old `asmcopy`, new `asmcopy`.
- Round 2: the exact reverse of round 1. Order: new `asmcopy`, old `asmcopy`, new `asmwrite`, old `asmwrite`, new `asmread`, old `asmread`, new `copy`, old `copy`, new `write`, old `write`, new `read`, old `read`.
- Every process gets the same arguments: 120 threads and the CPU list `0-119`. The binary pins thread number i to CPU i. `256M` gives each thread its own buffer of 256 MiB. Each process times 3 intervals of at least 500 ms each [Ref3].
- All 24 processes append to one file, `threads120.csv`.
- No wait comes before this part or between two processes. On 2026-11-13 the last one-thread process started at 18:17:20 UTC and the first of the 24 processes at 18:17:21 UTC [Ref2].
- ra.sh holds these four lines and the function `one` with the same text [Ref8].
Line 79 appends the load averages and the UTC time after the last process to `probe.txt`. Line 80 prints the result folder.
